Alphabet uses the operational control approach to define its organizational boundary for GHG emissions accounting.
Alphabet accounts for all emissions from operations over which it has operational control, including data centers, offices, and other assets.
Alphabet's GHG inventory includes all seven GHGs addressed by the Kyoto Protocol where relevant: CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6, and NF3.
Perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), and nitrogen trifluoride (NF3) are not emitted as a result of Alphabet's operations.
Alphabet reports emissions in metric tons per gas and in metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e), with biogenic emissions reported as tCO2 only.
In 2024, Alphabet stopped reporting a scope 3 (Other categories) metric that previously aggregated emissions from category 2, category 11, and category 12.
Alphabet determined that category 12 (End-of-life treatment of sold products) is not relevant and is no longer included in its inventory boundary.
Emissions from category 11 (Use of sold products) are not a material component of total scope 3 emissions.

Category 1 (Purchased goods and services) includes upstream emissions from manufacturing consumer devices and spare parts, Alphabet's food program, and additional goods and services purchased for operations.
We calculate upstream emissions from purchased fuel, steam, heating, and cooling using 2024 DEFRA UK Government GHG Conversion Factors.
We calculate emissions from upstream electricity by country using the 2024 IEA Emission Factors.

We calculate emissions from electricity transmission and distribution losses using grid loss values and emission factors derived from the 2024 IEA Emission Factors and, for the United States, the 2025 EPA eGRID Emission Factors.
For upstream electricity, we calculate emissions using scope 2 market-based data by using the remaining electricity not addressed by renewable energy.
For electricity transmission and distribution losses, we use the market-based method to account for EACs that we've purchased to cover a portion of grid losses.
Category 4: Upstream transportation and distribution includes emissions generated primarily from the transportation and warehousing of our consumer products and data center equipment.
We include the optional activity of upstream emissions of employee commuting using the distance-based method.
We survey our employees to determine typical commuting patterns and apply these patterns to our global employee population.

We calculate electricity procured from renewable sources (%) on an annual basis by dividing the megawatt-hours of renewable electricity procured by the total megawatt-hours of electricity consumed by our global operations.
Renewable electricity procured includes contractual instruments, on-site renewable electricity generation, and renewable electricity in the electric grids where our facilities are located.

To achieve our 100% renewable energy match, we first consider both our on-site renewable electricity generation and the renewable electricity already in the electric grids where our facilities are located.
We then procure renewable electricity through contractual instruments to achieve our 100% renewable energy match.
Water withdrawal is based on actual metered or invoiced data when it's available.

At offices where actual metered or invoiced data isn't available, water withdrawal is estimated using facility square footage and internally developed water withdrawal intensity factors by office type.
At data centers where actual data isn't available, water withdrawal is estimated using engineering principles.
Water discharge is based on actual metered or invoiced data when it's available.

Where actual domestic wastewater discharge data isn't available, an industry-standard 90% discharge flow factor is applied to a facility's domestic water withdrawal to estimate domestic water discharge.
A 0% discharge flow factor is applied to a facility's irrigation water withdrawal to estimate irrigation water discharge.
Carbon-free energy technologies include solar, wind, geothermal, hydropower, and nuclear.
The reporting boundary for GHG emissions, energy, and water metrics is Alphabet, globally.

Alphabet utilizes the operational control approach, as defined by the GHG Protocol, to establish relevant operations for emissions, energy, and water metrics at Alphabet's owned and leased data centers, offices, and other assets.
Alphabet uses the most up-to-date emission factors available at the time of their emissions inventory calculation.
Alphabet calculates emissions by multiplying relevant activity data by the applicable emission factors and global warming potentials (GWPs) where applicable.
The emissions from category 11 (Use of sold products) are not a material component of total scope 3 emissions.
Category 1: Purchased goods and services includes upstream emissions generated from manufacturing consumer devices and spare parts.
Alphabet uses a combination of the average-data method and spend-based method to calculate supply chain emissions.

Alphabet performs third-party-verified Life Cycle Assessments (LCAs) in accordance with ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 to calculate supply chain emissions generated from manufacturing consumer devices and spare parts.

To calculate emissions generated from the REWS food program, Alphabet uses LCA emission factors from WRI's Cool Food Pledge Calculator and annual procurement volumes from San Francisco Bay Area offices.
Alphabet collects well-to-wheel (WTW) emissions data for transportation emissions, calculated based on fuel use or weight-distance data.

Where actual logistics provider emissions data isn't available, Alphabet calculates WTW emissions using emission factors from the 2024 Global Logistics Emissions Council (GLEC) framework v3.1 or EPA SmartWay carrier performance data.

Alphabet calculates employee commuting emissions using mode-specific WTT emission factors from the 2024 DEFRA UK Government GHG Conversion Factors and TTW emission factors from the 2025 EPA Emission Factors for Greenhouse Gas Inventories.
Category 11: Use of sold products includes direct use-phase emissions generated by Google's consumer devices sold in the reporting period that directly consume electricity during use.
Category 11 emissions also include the optional activity of upstream electricity emissions of consumer devices by using LCA emission factors.
Alphabet performs LCAs for sold products that are in accordance with ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 and are third-party reviewed.
The LCA results for sold products are published on Google's Sustainability Reports webpage.

As of January 2023, Alphabet uses an updated energy savings calculation methodology to account for changes in common HVAC sizes and efficiencies, applying the respective energy savings percentages to Nest thermostats in North America and in European countries.
Poland's total electricity consumption was approximately 160 TWh in 2023.
Alphabet uses a 25-year estimated lifespan for solar panels in both annual and lifetime emissions reduction methods.
The estimated annual enabled emissions reduction takes into account solar installations enabled by Solar API prior to 2024, dating back to 2022, to calculate the total impact in 2024 alone.
Google uses an AI prediction model to estimate the expected fuel or energy consumption for each route option when users request driving directions.

To estimate operational emissions from electricity consumption of running workloads, Google used a one-month sample of observed machine power data from its entire TPU fleet, applying Google's 2023 average fleetwide carbon intensity.
To estimate embodied emissions from manufacturing, transportation, and retirement of TPU hardware, Google performed a life-cycle assessment of the hardware.
Data center construction emissions were estimated based on Google's disclosed 2023 carbon footprint.
